catalog_quote: 4.0. Suprasegmentals and Stress There is no strong evidence for stress features in Berta. However, while testing vowel qualities, it seemed that stress could be the cause for some vowel quality changes which I could not account for otherwise (see also section 3.2. Vowels). Example 32 ʃap’úθa ‘hit’ [ʃɐˈp’ʊ́θa] ~ [ʃuˈp’ʊ́θa] Another example is the word for ‘fast’: Example 33 [manˈdaŋ] ~ [mɨnˈdaŋ] As can be seen, stress is not expressed through pitch differences, as the stressed syllables in the examples have different tones. Still, this has not been investigated and is probably a field with interesting discoveries yet to be made. 4.1. Tone Berta is a tone language with two tones, high tone (H) and low tone (L). In a few instances there is a falling tone, and even less often, a rising one. These contours can be explained as a combination of high and low tone together on one tone bearing unit (TBU). While high tone and low tone can appear in any environment, the falling tone is restricted to the last syllable, and appears most often in Arabic loan words. The tone differentiates lexical as well as grammatical meaning.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Berta is analysed as a two-tone (H/L) language; the author finds no firm evidence of word stress, suspects a non-pitch prominence (marked on the second syllable in her two phonetic examples) that may condition vowel reduction, and states that stress placement has not been investigated. No position rule is given. (The older sketch, Triulzi, Dafallah & Bender 1976: 521, instead calls stress 'distinctive' with tone only possibly so, and says vowel length and high tone partly correlate with stress.)
new_statements.exceptions: None; only that word-initial /a/ may reduce to [ə] in a 'non-prominent syllable' (sec. 3.2), and that Arabic loans keep a falling tone / H tone where Arabic has stress (sec. 4.1; Ali et al. 2010: 78).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms; the two examples are isolated words with phonetic stress marks. Tone, not stress, is the described lexical/grammatical prosodic contrast.
new_statements.identity_note: Neudorf 2016 describes mainly the Mayu dialect of Berta (Asosa area, Ethiopia), with notes on Fadashi and Undulu; Glottolog treats these as dialects under bert1248 (Fadashi and Undu also have their own ISO codes/Glottolog entries as 'Berta languages': fada1236 Fadashi, undu1236? not verified here). Triulzi/Dafallah/Bender 1976 describe Undu with reference to Mayu and Fadashi. Neudorf 2021 covers the Wabosh (Fabosh) dialect and says only that tone is little studied there.

sources.note: Sec. 4.0 'Suprasegmentals and Stress' (p. 22): 'There is no strong evidence for stress features in Berta'; stress suspected only as a cause of some vowel-quality variation (exx. [ʃɐˈp'ʊ́θa]~[ʃuˈp'ʊ́θa] 'hit', [manˈdaŋ]~[mɨnˈdaŋ] 'fast', both marked with stress on the 2nd syllable); 'stress is not expressed through pitch differences'; 'this has not been investigated'. Sec. 4.1: Berta is a tone language with two tones (H, L), lexical and grammatical function. Sec. 3.2: word-initial /a/ may reduce to [ə] 'in a non-prominent syllable'. No placement rule given.
